title: Trump Authorizes Private Companies to Hack Foreign Cybercriminals in Major Policy Shift
excerpt: A presidential memo creates a new federal program allowing vetted US companies to conduct offensive cyberattacks against foreign criminal networks, raising questions about oversight, liability, and unintended consequences.
body:
• President Trump signed a memo Wednesday authorizing vetted private companies to conduct cyberattacks against foreign cybercriminal networks under federal oversight.
  • The program allows companies to surveil foreign criminals and disrupt their networks, a role historically reserved for US law enforcement, intelligence, and military agencies.
  • Former officials warn the program could create "cyber privateers" operating without clear coordination, risking collateral damage and legal liability for participating companies.
  • The Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security will oversee the program, with extra legal scrutiny required for any activity directed at US persons.

A New Role for the Private Sector

The Trump administration is enlisting private companies to conduct offensive cyberattacks on foreign cybercriminals, a significant escalation in the government's approach to cyber threats that experts say could carry serious legal and operational risks.

https://x.com/TrumpsPortfolio/status/2087936270181818816

President Trump signed a memo on Wednesday creating a new federal program that gives vetted companies a direct role in hacking operations that have historically been the exclusive domain of agencies like the FBI, the NSA, and US Cyber Command.

Under the program, participating companies can use cyber tools to surveil foreign criminal groups and disrupt their networks, operating under what the memo describes as the "control and oversight" of the federal government. The program's scope is limited to foreign criminal organizations — not foreign governments.

"American businesses' innovative capabilities have historically been underutilized in efforts to identify and disrupt criminal networks operating in cyberspace."

— Presidential memo

Critics Warn of 'Cyber Privateers'

The program drew immediate warnings from former national security officials who compared it to the historical practice of governments issuing letters of marque to private ships — essentially, creating state-sanctioned pirates.

"The real risk is that you end up with a bunch of cyber privateers running around without any clear coordination or direction at the federal level," said Andrew Schoka, a former Army officer at US Cyber Command.

Deconflicting cyber operations — ensuring that different entities don't accidentally disrupt each other's operations or hit the same targets — is already a major challenge among federal agencies. Adding private companies with significant capabilities and speed makes that problem harder, Schoka said.

Potential Benefits and Risks

Proponents argue the program could help address a severe capacity gap. Chinese government-backed hackers outnumber FBI cyber personnel 50-to-1, according to former FBI director Christopher Wray. Offloading some counter-criminal operations to private companies could free up federal resources to focus on nation-state threats.

"Having private sector help to counter cyber criminals allows the US to disrupt more groups and frees up agencies like FBI and Cyber Command to focus more on countering nation states like China," said Cynthia Kaiser, a former senior FBI cyber official.

But Kaiser cautioned that "the devil is in the details," noting that companies will need explicit information about liability protections, the types of government oversight involved, and how operations against foreign criminals using US infrastructure would be handled.

Collateral Damage Concerns

Chris Wysopal, co-founder of cybersecurity firm Veracode, warned that government-sanctioned hacking by private firms could have unintended consequences. Targeting a data center in a foreign country to go after scammers could inadvertently affect hospitals or other critical infrastructure sharing the same servers.

Foreign governments may also view employees of participating companies who travel abroad as legitimate targets for detention or questioning, Wysopal said.

Oversight Questions Remain

The memo assigns oversight of the program to the departments of Justice and Homeland Security. Any program activity directed at a US person must undergo additional legal scrutiny, including review by the Justice Department.

But Jason Kikta, a former Cyber Command official, said the memo lacks a clear process for ensuring that cyber operations uphold civil liberties. "There is no clear oversight or review process on the determinations that will be made by unnamed political appointees," Kikta said. "This order pushes liability on to the companies."

The program builds on Executive Order 14390, signed in March 2026, which laid out a broader framework for enlisting private sector capabilities in the government's offense-oriented approach to cyber threats.
